title: Gravity as an Elastic Rope: The Secret of Wide Binary Stars
oneliner: New research shows that in wide binary systems, stars are bound by gravity that’s too strong—like an invisible rope that tightens as they pull apart.
description: Astronomers ruled out all possible interference: hidden satellites, instrument errors, different stellar ages and compositions. Even in flawless pairs, orbital speeds exceed Newton’s predictions, and the gravitational “rope” turns out to be more elastic than expected. This effect supports MOND, wher
abstract: Wide binary stars are two stars held together by gravity. At large distances, they move as if gravity is stronger than expected. Even hidden companions can’t explain it, which supports a new theory (MOND). Imagine a rock on a rubber band: when you spin it, it doesn’t fly off—the rubber band pulls it back. Just like that, gravity seems to strengthen at vast distances.
threads: Два фигуриста на бескрайнем льду. Их танец едва заметен — но что-то подо льдом разгоняет их быстрее, чем положено. Именно так ведёт себя гравитация в широких двойных звёздах: данные Gaia трижды подтвердили упрямую аномалию. Если эффект реален, тёмная материя может оказаться миражом, а учебники физики затрещат по швам.

title: Robot Tour Guides: Why a Pair Is Better Than One
oneliner: A duo of a robot and a hologram partner makes a museum tour not just a spectacle but a way to absorb facts more deeply, especially for women.
description: Researchers turned the tour into a show: a real robot guide got a holographic assistant. Comparing a solo format, a projection, and a mixed pair on 30 visitors showed that interest was high in all, but recall improved for women with the duo. Participants unanimously preferred the lively conversation
abstract: Imagine a museum tour where you're accompanied by two guides: one a real robot, and the other a virtual companion appearing like a hologram. This duo creates a sense of lively conversation. An unusual effect: women remembered information better with the virtual partner, while men showed no change. But absolutely everyone preferred this duo over a solitary robot. Perhaps museums should match guides to the visitor's mindset?

title: Smart Filter for Secret Keys: Autoencoder vs. Noise
oneliner: An autoencoder removes noise from a radio signal, helping two devices obtain a shared reliable secret key.
description: A new method uses an autoencoder—a program that learns to clear noise from a signal, like wiping a fogged-up window. That way, two phones see an identical random picture of the radio channel and can craft a shared secret key, even in heavy interference. The keys turn out stronger, with almost zero e
abstract: Two devices, like smartphones, can create a shared secret key by listening to radio noise. But interference often makes their keys mismatched. A new method uses a 'smart cleaner' — picture an eraser that scrubs away noise distortions while keeping the true signal. This boosted reliability and slashed errors. Could this kind of cleanup make keys flawless?

title: How to Pack a Million Shades into a Tiny Box
oneliner: The method packs millions of shades, grouping them like candies in a box, so video chips instantly deliver a smooth picture.
description: Virtual worlds are made of colored dots whose shade depends on the viewing angle. Storing this data is a gluttonous task. Engineers proposed compressing them by grouping similar shades, like candies in a box. The graphics card instantly extracts the average color with a tiny correction, without sacr
abstract: 3D scenes created from photos remember how each point looks under different lighting. To keep them from being too 'heavy', the authors came up with a compression method like a smart suitcase: colors are neatly grouped and packed, then unpacked almost instantly using the GPU. Could we now store all the world’s movies in a pocket?

title: The Secret of Faint Light: How to Map Invisible Galaxies
oneliner: Astronomers have learned to determine distances to galaxies that cannot be seen individually.
description: Scientists have developed a method to infer the spatial distribution of millions of faint galaxies from their collective glow. They trained a computer program on virtual models of the universe, and the program learned to predict distances with high accuracy. This will help study the history of the u
abstract: Astronomers have learned to determine distances to distant galaxies from their overall scattered light—like understanding how far away a crowd is by its noise. The method gives very high accuracy and will allow searching for traces of dark matter and the evolution of the Universe where before we saw only blurry glow. What other secrets does this 'fog' hide?
threads: Тусклое свечение космического фона — не брак оптики, а хор из 90% галактик, не видимых поодиночке. Подобно чтению палимпсеста, мы научились разделять этот свет на слои времени и определять расстояние до каждого 'голоса' с точностью менее 1%. Однажды это позволит разглядеть самые первые звёзды Вселенной.

title: Echo of the Big Bang: How Invisible Particles Sound
oneliner: In the ancient light of the Universe, new traces of superheavy particles that lived only an instant after the Big Bang have been found.
description: Two quantum fields in the early Universe turned out to be much more strongly coupled than previously thought. Their mutual influence amplified the signal imprinted in the cosmic microwave background many times over. Now, using these 'beats,' we can search for dark matter candidates and explain the b
abstract: The first moments after the Big Bang determined how matter is distributed in the Universe. Scientists have found a way to describe what happens when several fields interact simultaneously during this period. If the fields strongly influence each other, irregularities amplify—like an avalanche triggered by the slightest push. This helps us understand the nature of giant black holes.
threads: В первые мгновения после Большого взрыва Вселенная была коллайдером с энергией, недоступной земным технологиям. Её эхо хранит следы тяжёлых частиц. Как мощный блендер, сильное смешивание полей взбило эти сигналы до гигантских амплитуд. Новый математический аппарат позволяет их уловить — и, возможно, выйти на след тёмной материи.

title: Self-Taught Algorithm: How to Hear a Melody from Noise
oneliner: A new adaptive data recovery method tunes its own parameters, achieving near-perfect accuracy even with rough initial errors.
description: A new adaptive method automatically picks parameters to reconstruct a signal from scattered data. It works like a musician tuning an instrument by ear to blend with the orchestra, despite the noise. The algorithm adjusts its internal model on the fly. This is especially valuable when restoring image
abstract: How do you recover a signal from incomplete data if the algorithm's settings are off? Imagine a radio receiver that tunes itself to the clear frequency. The new method works the same way: it automatically refines parameters using already gathered information, and after a rough start, achieves near-perfect results. Isn't this a step toward autonomous image processing systems?

title: How to read an enemy in the sky in seconds
oneliner: Combat algorithms learn to make decisions from scraps of data, honestly acknowledging uncertainty.
description: A new air combat algorithm acts like an experienced goalkeeper: from the first patchy radar signals, it predicts the target type and maneuvers, not afraid to admit doubts. In tests — 88% accuracy for class, 93% for intentions.
abstract: In a fast air battle, pilots must instantly recognize threats and predict intentions. Traditional AI needs long data, which is risky. This method uses short data chunks, like guessing a story from a few pages. It identifies targets 88% correctly and intentions 93% correctly. Could everyday safety tech learn from this?

title: Black hole as a trampoline: why dust flies away
oneliner: Curved space around a black hole works like a trampoline: particles more often fly outward than fall in.
description: Scientists found out: due to space stretching, a black hole pulls in dust less often than thought. The curvature acts like a trampoline, flinging particles away. This explains the strange flickering of X-rays from Cygnus X-1 and helps test gravity strength through observations.
abstract: Picture a dust grain drifting in a whirlpool near a black hole's edge. Its motion is like a random dance through warped space. Surprisingly, it has a better chance of escaping than it would in normal space: near the horizon, space 'stretches' out, giving the particle more room to wander. This explains the twinkling of X-rays from black holes. Oddly enough, black holes sometimes help things avoid falling in, don't they?
threads: Чёрная дыра — не пылесос, а батут: кривизна статистически отбрасывает пылинки к космологическому горизонту. Это открытие меняет взгляд на аккрецию и обещает новый инструмент для проверки общей теории относительности — по временным рядам рентгеновской переменности.

title: Why Genes Disrupt the Family Tree
oneliner: Why gene stories don't match the evolution of species, and how a mathematical model helps unravel the tangle.
description: In evolution, genes don't always follow in the species' footsteps. Random loss of variants or direct exchange between unrelated species muddles the picture. Researchers built a simple model of these transfers to understand how often they create the illusion of a different kinship.
abstract: Why are genes from one species sometimes closer to genes from another? Blame horizontal transfer (gene jumps between species) or incomplete sorting (prolonged mixing within a species). Scientists calculated the probabilities of these events for two and three species and showed whether they can be told apart. Imagine a family tree tangled by 'adopted' genes.

title: The Mystery of the Torn Star: How a Corona Is Born
oneliner: A star torn apart by a black hole let us watch a mysterious hot corona ignite.
description: In 2024, astronomers observed in unprecedented detail how a supermassive black hole ripped a star apart, and how a hot 'corona'—a region where light gains colossal energy—was born from the debris. This discovery links the behavior of giant and tiny black holes, pointing to universal laws of matter i
abstract: Astronomers watched as a black hole tore apart a star (event TDE 2024aepd). Unusually, a powerful infrared 'excess' appeared just 40 days later — as if a fog around a lamp started glowing before the lamp itself. This is only the third such case — a mystery: do other similar disasters also hide their heat?
threads: В считанные недели после того, как чёрная дыра разрывает звезду, рождается горячая корона — область, где фотоны взмывают до рентгеновских энергий, словно оркестр берёт крещендо. Инфракрасный избыток, подобный низкому басу, разносит эхо переработанного излучения. Понимание этих процессов — ключ к разгадке роста сверхмассивных чёрных дыр и рождения галактик.

title: Disorder Gives Birth to Magnetic Vortices
oneliner: Scientists have for the first time observed how, in a mix of superconducting and ordinary grains, tangled magnetic vortices spontaneously appear when cooled.
description: In a new material resembling a mix of metal filings in glass, tiny magnetic vortices spontaneously appear when cooled to very low temperatures. They emerge not from an external magnet, but from the internal mismatch of superconducting regions. These vortices store information about how superconducti
abstract: Scientists have for the first time looked in detail at how, as a superconductor cools, microscopic vortices spontaneously arise — like tiny tornadoes inside the material. These vortices hold information about the very first instant of the transition to an ordered state. What else can these frozen imprints tell us about the birth of order from chaos?
threads: Космические струны — гипотетические складки пространства-времени — возможно, застыли в первые мгновения после Большого взрыва. Сегодня физики нашли их миниатюрное подобие в куске сверхпроводящей керамики. Запутанные магнитные вихри, самопроизвольно возникшие при охлаждении, — это отпечаток фазового перехода, словно фотография рождения порядка. Изучая их, мы, возможно, поймём, как Вселенная обретала структуру.

title: Magnetic Bridge Through Earth: Relay Boosts Communication
oneliner: Engineers found a way to speed up magnetic communication through the ground using a repeater.
description: Magnetic fields penetrate the ground where radio waves fail. A new method adds a repeater — a device that amplifies the signal — and allows precise calculation of how much faster data transfer becomes. The solutions will be useful in mines, subways, and underwater exploration.
abstract: Magnetic induction lets you communicate through the earth, like radio through air. To speed up the connection, a relay was added that catches and amplifies the signal. Getting its antenna in the right spot can dramatically boost speed—it's like finding the sweet spot for a Wi-Fi extender underground.

title: How a Self-Driving Car Builds a Map from Above
oneliner: Scientists trained a computer to piece together a road map from fragmented snapshots, sifting through possible variations.
description: The computer generates several draft maps and picks the best one, merging camera data as if looking out of different windows. This approach makes lane marking recognition reliable even in bad weather.
abstract: For a self-driving car to understand the road, it needs a top-down map, like a bird seeing everything from above. But piecing together such a map from multiple camera shots isn't easy. Scientists have devised a clever system that learns to draw an accurate road layout, much like an experienced cartographer, and even proposes several options, choosing the best one. Could it one day handle a traffic jam better than we do?

title: The Complexity of Crowds: Why Averages Fail
oneliner: CWMMSE measures complexity, seeing not the average picture, but the full diversity of hidden patterns.
description: CWMMSE measures the complexity of trajectory sets by grouping similar paths and assessing not only their entanglement but also the differences between groups. It turns out: a calm ocean is more complex than a stormy one due to hidden diversity of currents, and heart disease reduces not overall chaos
abstract: Conventional methods average out chaos, mistaking diversity for complexity. The new approach breaks data into typical scenarios and weighs them by complexity — in an orchestra, it’s not the loudness but the parts that matter. This flipped conclusions: a calm ocean turned out more complex than a stormy one, and heart disease reduces rhythm diversity. What’s more complex: a flock of birds or a line at the bank?

title: WanSong: Songs from Noise in One Step
oneliner: The WanSong neural network turns random noise into songs up to five minutes long with vocals and instruments.
description: WanSong works like a sculptor: it transforms noise into music by removing the excess step by step. Unlike other models, it creates multi-track songs straight away, with no intermediate stages, and automatically separates vocals and instruments. This makes editing easier.
abstract: The new WanSong model creates songs up to five minutes long, splitting them into voice and music right away. It’s like a chef who cooks a whole meal in one pot but serves each dish separately. Imagine how that’ll speed up music creation!

title: The Unheard Knock of Cement Reveals Its Nanostructure
oneliner: Scientists have for the first time registered unique vibrations in cement gel, revealing just how unevenly it’s assembled at the nanoscale.
description: The cement paste that binds concrete consists of tiny irregularly shaped particles. For a long time, it was unclear exactly how nanoscale heterogeneity affects the material's strength and thermal conductivity. A new study combined two high-precision techniques to 'hear' a unique signal—the boson pea
abstract: Hardened concrete isn't exactly solid: at the microscale, it resembles a frozen liquid. Such materials have a special 'vibrational signature' — the boson peak. For the first time, scientists have studied it in detail in cement stone and linked it to concrete durability. Imagine: from the barely perceptible trembling of nanometer-sized regions, you can predict how a bridge will withstand decades of loads.
threads: Представьте барабан, натянутый неравномерно: его звук выдаёт распределение напряжений. Бозонный пик в цементе — такой же «голос» наномира: частота ~1 ТГц раскрывает флуктуации жёсткости на наномасштабе. Управляя этим гулом, мы создадим бетон, который не ползёт веками — и однажды, возможно, отправится на Марс.

title: Ghost Echoes Make Radar More Precise
oneliner: A receiver defect that creates false reflections paradoxically improves radar clarity.
description: Radar signals are split into multiple frequencies. The slightest electronic imbalance spawns phantom copies of targets. Instead of suppressing them, they're used alongside the real ones—accuracy soars.
abstract: Imagine a radar that sees ghosts because of its own "cross-eyed" vision. Instead of correcting the eyesight, the new method leverages the distortion itself: like a detective who looks at a blurred photo and picks out the real figures and their doppelgangers. This way, even faint targets can be caught amid the noise. What else might we spot in a "corrupted" signal?

title: Radar Sculptor: How Radio Waves Sculpt a Drone's Portrait
oneliner: The technology turns reflected signals into a three-dimensional sculpture, revealing a drone's shape and movement.
description: Scientists trained radar to reconstruct a drone's appearance and notice the slightest changes — down to a light payload. The method outperforms optics in fog and darkness.
abstract: Imagine a radar that doesn't just detect an object, but draws its 3D portrait: position in space, tilt, and even shape. Scientists created a system where a base station with antennas illuminates a flying drone with radio waves and from the reflections reconstructs its “electromagnetic point cloud”. This helps track drones more accurately. But what if the drone starts maneuvering too sharply?

title: Radar Without Ghosts: A New 'Melody' Against False Targets
oneliner: Engineers composed a radio pulse 'melody' that rids radar of ghost targets while keeping the picture sharp.
description: To cut costs, radar signal processing is 'compressed', but ghost targets appear—like off-key notes in a poor recording. Previous pulse designs gave either clarity with many ghosts or purity at the cost of smearing. The new SC-EFM modulation is a distinct waveform that almost eliminates 'false notes'
abstract: When a radar cuts corners on measurements, false 'ghosts' appear in its readings. Scientists crafted a signal that, like a musical chord, silences the ghosts and keeps real targets from blending together. It’s like picking out each voice in a noisy crowd. What matters more: seeing a mirage on the cheap, or spending a bit more to see the truth?

title: How the Brain Conducts Attention: A Meditation Model
oneliner: A new model explains how the brain manages attention: like an experienced conductor, it learns to quickly notice distractions and gently return to the main focus.
description: Scientists simulated meditation on a computer, identifying four states: focus on breathing, mind wandering, awareness of distraction, and return. Comparing beginners and experts revealed that experienced meditators recognize distractions faster and shift more smoothly. The model links subjective exp
abstract: Scientists built a computer model of how the brain sustains attention during meditation. It shifts between focusing on the breath, mind-wandering, and noticing distraction—like a flashlight that realizes it’s pointing the wrong way and corrects its beam. The model recreated behavior of both novices and experts. Doesn’t it evoke a theater where the mind is both actor and audience?

title: Compressing networks: when roads become points
oneliner: Scientists found a clever way to compress numeric networks: lines become dots, and barely noticeable fluctuations are discarded.
description: A new method for packing numeric maps (like road networks with traffic). First, the map is transformed: roads become nodes, and intersections become edges between them. Then numeric values are decomposed into simple waves, and weak ones are discarded. The rest are encoded very densely. A smoothness
abstract: Imagine a road map peppered with traffic jams. To send the jam data compactly without losing the street layout, scientists turn streets into points in a new network, connecting them if the streets intersect. Then they smooth out the jams—like ironing wrinkles from fabric—and compress. This trick offers a predictability score: how easy it is to squeeze the data. Picture the jams themselves whispering where you can save on traffic!

title: Flying Radio Mirror: A Drone That Steers Its Own Signal
oneliner: A flying radio mirror adjusts in real time to the drone's shaking, keeping the signal pristine.
description: A prototype smart surface on a drone acts as a self-aiming mirror for radio signals. Even in flight, when the drone shakes, the mirror predicts displacements and instantly reorients itself—keeping the link perfect.
abstract: Picture a drone with a smart mirror that catches radio waves and beams them straight to your phone. This mirror can tilt on its own to cancel out the drone’s shaking and wobbling in midair. Scientists have assembled such a flying reflector for the first time and proven it works in real-world conditions—wind, vibrations, and all. Could these helper drones be the future of mobile connectivity?

title: How Robots Negotiate the Noisy Airwaves
oneliner: Reliable radio communication between robots improves movement accuracy and saves energy.
description: Random delays in the wireless network confuse robots. Engineers tested different transmission modes in a 5G network: reliable signal delivery improved accuracy by 51.5% compared to the usual approach.
abstract: When robots work together, wireless dropouts can ruin everything—like musicians in an orchestra hearing each other with a delay. Scientists found a way to tune robot motion so that even with interference they act in harmony and don't waste energy. It's as if a conductor gives each one the perfect rhythm. What if cars communicated this way on the road?

title: How a Bent Crystal Turns Sound into Rotation
oneliner: Scientists have theoretically shown that in curved crystalline membranes, sound vibrations generate a weak but measurable torque due to a special quantum viscosity.
description: In a flat membrane, bending vibrations usually don't lead to rotation. But if the membrane is slightly curved, even a faint sound can make it slowly turn. Theorists calculated that in the magnetic crystal α-RuCl3, this effect produces a torque of about 2×10⁻²² Newton-meters, which can already be det
abstract: In a flat membrane, bending waves don't produce any special friction—the Hall viscosity. But if the membrane is curved, bending causes twisting, and a tiny torque appears. For a few layers of α-RuCl₃, it's estimated at 10⁻²² N·m—already detectable with instruments. Could curvature be the secret to measuring hidden quantum forces?
threads: В крошечной изогнутой мембране из магнитного кристалла звуковые волны не просто колеблются — они начинают вращаться. Кривизна играет роль дирижёра: без неё холловская вязкость — таинственная «смазка», не создающая трения, — остаётся безмолвной. Так рождается постоянный угловой момент, измеримый теми же датчиками, что ловят гравитационные волны. Мы на пороге тепловых гироскопов без движущихся деталей — только геометрия и квантовая фаза.

title: AI Plans Radiation Therapy in Two Minutes
oneliner: Artificial intelligence independently and accurately builds a radiation plan for a cancerous tumor from daily scans—in just two minutes.
description: Scientists have created an AI agent that fully automates the daily preparation for radiation therapy. It processes a CT scan, identifies tumor boundaries, calculates doses, and suggests settings—all in two minutes. A doctor supervises the key steps. As a result, treatment speeds up, the burden on me
abstract: A smart autopilot for radiation therapy: from a daily 3D scan, it builds a tumor map and treatment plan in two minutes, while the doctor can always step in. Could a single AI assistant soon handle all types of cancer without a hitch?

title: Why photo enhancement software fails on unfamiliar images
oneliner: Photo cleanup programs stumble on unfamiliar images because they take steps in the wrong direction. But a quick tweak with a few examples corrects the course.
description: Photo enhancement software often ruins frames with unusual blur or noise. The culprit isn't a general error, but the algorithm's misdirected steps—it veers off course. By showing it a few examples of proper cleanup, you can adjust its path without a complete overhaul.
abstract: When restoring images, ready-made noise 'cleaners' are often used, but they can make mistakes if the picture is unlike those they were trained on. The authors measured this mismatch error and showed how to adjust the cleaner to new conditions. This allows even a couple of examples to noticeably improve the result — like glasses that automatically adjust their prescription to your vision.

title: A Map That Isn't Afraid to Admit: 'I Don't Know'
oneliner: Robots build a map with guaranteed accuracy, openly admitting where the data is unreliable.
description: Scientists have found a way to fuse data from a group of robots so that the final map directly flags dubious areas. The method works regardless of sensor quality or communication links between the machines.
abstract: Robots exploring unknown territory swap tiny blips of confidence. As these signals merge, they build a shared map with guaranteed accuracy. Where data is scarce, the map stays silent, leaving white spots. The more they chatter, the fewer the spots. Like a team whispering to make sure no vital detail slips by.

title: How Spite Replenishes Resources
oneliner: When a resource replenishes slowly, spite unexpectedly allows it to recover, then gives way to fairness.
description: In repeated negotiations over a shared resource, the speed of its replenishment decides everything. Rapid growth encourages fairness, slow growth creates a paradoxical cycle: spite temporarily takes over, but this allows the resource to accumulate and fairness to return.
abstract: Imagine a shared garden: if fruit ripens quickly, it's better to share fairly; if it's slow, greed emerges. Scientists modeled how two people negotiate over such renewable resources and saw: fast resource growth leads to fairness, slow growth to stinginess. It seems nature dictates how generous we are to each other.

title: Snapshot of the Invisible: How They Guessed the Portrait of a Black Hole
oneliner: A black hole's portrait is an image assembled from sparse signals and physical intuition, like a city map guessed from a few scattered lights.
description: In 2019, astrophysicists revealed the shadow of a black hole in the galaxy M87, pieced together from fragments of data from eight radio dishes. A direct snapshot is impossible: the portrait is woven from signals, gravitational theory, and computational guesswork—like a map of an invisible city.
abstract: Imagine reconstructing a portrait from a few blurry pixels — you can get different faces. Same with the first photo of a black hole: from sparse data, many different images were possible. Scientists picked one, but the key discovery is that all the variants looked similar, confirming the shadow's reality. How many faces are hiding in your fuzzy photos?
threads: Когда в 2019 году показали снимок чёрной дыры, многие решили, что это фотография. На самом деле, это симфония, собранная по обрывкам партитуры. Восемь антенн по всей планете уловили лишь несколько «нот» от плазмы вокруг M87*. Алгоритмы, словно дирижёры, достроили мелодию — каждый по-своему. Итог — усреднение трёх версий. Следующее поколение добавит космические «уши», и тогда, возможно, мы услышим голос бездны в полную силу.

title: Where Are You? Radio Waves Know the Answer
oneliner: Like a sensitive ear, your phone picks up the unique pattern of radio waves in a room—and from that, figures out exactly where you're standing.
description: Indoors, a radio signal behaves like a note sung in a concert hall: reflections create a one-of-a-kind melody for each spot. A listener program memorizes these invisible chords and uses them to locate you more precisely than GPS. This technology promises navigation in subways and smart factories.
abstract: Imagine your phone determines your location by how radio signals bounce off the walls. Scientists teach systems to recognize these reflections, but environmental and device changes get in the way — like trying to recognize a friend's voice in a noisy café through different phones. How do you teach a machine to 'hear' position despite the interference?

title: How Robots Chart a Course Through a Galaxy of Errors
oneliner: A subtle helm in the digital brain keeps robots from losing their grip, even as the world shifts around them.
description: Robots drop objects when their neural network gets scrambled. Scientists spotted a galaxy in those signals: successful and faulty commands separated like safe and perilous space. So they embedded a helm that steers signals back on course in real time. Now, even with a shaky camera, the grasp holds f
abstract: Robots often fail when facing unexpected hiccups—like a shifting camera or noisy data. Scientists peeked into their 'brains' and spotted clear signals that control steadiness. By tweaking those signals, much like correcting a skid with the wheel, they made the machines more reliable. Could robots one day outpace animals in agility?

title: How Noise Creates Diversity
oneliner: Random noise can reinforce, not erase, diversity in a population.
description: A new study flips the script: in the Hawks and Doves game, random fluctuations don’t average out behavior but split the population into warriors and peacemakers, preserving this divide for the long haul.
abstract: In evolution, there are flexible strategies, where an individual acts according to the situation, and rigid ones, where each individual has its own role. This work showed that in small groups, random fluctuations make division of roles advantageous, rather than universality. So why does nature so often prefer a team of specialists?

title: Smart Circuits for Clear Signals
oneliner: A new tuning algorithm for radio transmitters turns budget hardware into speed record-holders.
description: When a transmitter has multiple antennas, they need to be matched, otherwise the signal is lost. Scientists developed a method for tuning internal circuits that squeezes maximum speed even from mediocre components.

title: How to Teach AI Not to Confuse Similar MRI Scans
oneliner: Scientists have proposed a method that helps artificial intelligence analyze medical images more accurately, even when they look identical.
description: Typically, during training, AI compares paired data and treats everything else as different. But in medicine, two scans can be very similar even though they belong to different patients. This confuses the AI, leading to errors. The new MseaCL system uses doctors' text reports to understand how simil
abstract: Think of a library where books are shelved by topic. A typical algorithm assumed that any books not side by side were on completely different subjects, blurring similar ones together. Scientists taught the AI to gauge how related the text descriptions actually are, so it could spot connections more accurately. As a result, the accuracy of recognizing children’s brain tumors jumped by a quarter. What else is hiding in medical archives if we learn to look smarter?

title: Galactic Chemical Clocks: Why They Tick Faster on the Outskirts
oneliner: Scientists discovered that the ratio of yttrium to magnesium in a star can serve as an age indicator, but these 'clocks' tick at different speeds depending on the location in the Galaxy.
description: Astronomers found a way to determine the age of stars by the ratio of two chemical elements: yttrium and magnesium. But these 'clocks' are not universal — on the outskirts of the Milky Way they tick faster, while in its thick disk they almost grind to a halt. The discovery is based on analysis of 73
abstract: The ratio of two chemical elements in stars is like a clock ticking away the age. But its pace changes from place to place in the Galaxy: for stars similar to the Sun in composition, young ones contain less yttrium, while old ones have more. In more 'enriched' stars, the difference fades away. What forces wind these celestial clocks in different ways?
threads: Звёздный хронометр оказался с географией: во внешнем диске Галактики химические часы на иттрии и магнии спешат, а в толстом — еле ползут. Это открытие рушит миф об универсальном методе датировки и рисует Млечный Путь как оркестр, где каждая секция играет в своём темпе. В будущем многомерные модели машинного обучения восстановят всю историю Галактики по этим разноголосым партитурам.

title: Dark matter barely interacts with neutrinos
oneliner: Light from distant quasars shows that dark matter and neutrinos interact negligibly.
description: Light from distant quasars, passing through hydrogen clouds, reveals that dark matter and neutrinos barely notice each other. This is the tightest constraint yet, bolstering our cosmological model.
abstract: Scientists searched for 'traces' of dark matter interacting with neutrinos by analyzing light from distant quasars, much like reading history from tree rings. It turned out that even if such an interaction exists, it is very weak—the tightest constraint to date. So, is dark matter even more invisible than we thought?
threads: Миллиарды лет свет квазаров нёс сквозь космос ноты водородной партитуры. Астрофизики прислушались, надеясь уловить дуэт тёмной материи и нейтрино. Но расслышали лишь абсолютное молчание: взаимодействие оказалось как минимум в сотню раз слабее, чем предполагали смелые гипотезы. Этот предел не просто отсекает модные теории — он заставляет по-новому взглянуть на скрытую жизнь Вселенной.

title: Gene Map Predicts Breast Cancer Outcomes
oneliner: A mathematical cartographer drew a map of the genetic city and found the neighborhood where aggressive breast cancer becomes vulnerable.
description: For a thousand women with breast cancer, scientists created an activity map of genes—each gene like a house, its work the life inside. The mathematical cartographer revealed hidden neighborhoods invisible to standard tests. It turned out that patients from 'quiet' neighborhoods with aggressive cance
abstract: Using an unusual mathematical approach, like mapping terrain, scientists found hidden groups of breast cancer patients. One group, despite having an aggressive tumor type, lived longer thanks to a special molecular profile that responded better to treatment. This is how gene geometry points to new ways to save lives.

title: Rotating Black Holes: Invisible Hairdryers for Cosmic Dust
oneliner: Factoring in the spin of tiny black holes revealed they can heat interstellar dust far more effectively, acting like miniature hair dryers.
description: Primordial black holes — microscopic objects possibly left over from the universe’s birth, are candidates for dark matter. Their rapid spin greatly amplifies radiation, and like a hair dryer blasting hot air, they heat cosmic dust. This allowed a more precise estimate of their abundance: no more tha
abstract: Tiny primordial black holes could be part of dark matter. They heat interstellar dust via Hawking radiation (energy emission), especially if they spin fast. The type of dark matter distribution in a galaxy (halo profile) affects how tight the constraints are: the isothermal model gives the strictest limits. Silicate (rocky) dust heats up more than graphite (carbon-based) dust. For fast-spinning holes, their possible share of dark matter is no more than 0.01%.
threads: Межзвёздная пыль — триллионы микротермометров, разбросанных по Галактике. Они чутко реагируют на малейший нагрев, выдавая местоположение испаряющихся чёрных дыр. Учёт спина показал: даже слабое вращение умножает излучение и затягивает петлю ограничений. Возможно, скоро инфракрасные карты неба станут окном в природу тёмной материи.

title: A Colorful World Through a Single Pixel
oneliner: Adaptive mask switching helps a single pixel distinguish hundreds of shades without expensive optics.
description: Cameras that distinguish hundreds of shades are expensive. A new approach captures such images with a simple sensor: the measurement sequence is tailored to the scene, boosting clarity in visible and near-infrared light.
abstract: Spectral images help monitor fields and forests, but the necessary cameras are expensive. Scientists proposed making them with a single pixel and clever light patterns that adapt to the frame, like a painter changing brushes. The result is clear color images at no extra cost. Imagine a camera that sees more finely than the eye, almost for free?

title: World in Flickers: How a Camera Assembles an Image from Flashes
oneliner: From a stream of flickers, scientists assembled a detailed picture of the Earth's surface.
description: Regular cameras capture frames. Event-based ones only detect changes in light. Scientists have shown how to assemble a sharp image from these changes, like a puzzle of light shards. Tests on the ISS confirmed: the method distinguishes clouds, islands, and landscape.
abstract: Event cameras see only flickers—where it gets brighter or darker. Researchers turned these flickering sparks into a sharp image, like assembling a puzzle from trembling fireflies. The method teases out the big picture, smoothing away the jitter. Think: could you recognize a room just by the shadows of a candle flame?

title: Why Not Every Contact Leads to Illness
oneliner: A new model accounts for infection depending on the amount of virus, which changes over time.
description: Scientists created a model where infection depends on the 'age of infection'—the time since the virus entered the body. This age determines how much virus can be transmitted upon contact. The larger the dose, the higher the chance of getting sick. Such a model predicts epidemic development more accu
abstract: This model takes into account 'failed' contacts (you were near a sick person but didn’t get infected) and how long a person has been infected—this affects the amount of virus. It’s like standing in the rain: how wet you get depends on the downpour’s strength and how long you’re out there. Why do some people catch it and others don’t? It’s all about the dose and the timing.

title: Lightweight AI for Space Communications: More Accurate and Efficient
oneliner: A tiny AI model predicts radio signal distortions on a satellite, using almost no power.
description: Interference disrupts satellite communications. A new power-efficient AI running directly on board accurately catches signal distortions with minimal energy consumption. This will bring internet to the most remote corners.
abstract: For the future internet to fly through satellites (6G), they need an economical 'brain' to assess signal quality. Regular AI methods are too power-hungry for space. Scientists have created a lightweight neural network that processes the signal directly on board, saving energy like a solar-powered watch. Could this approach speed up the advent of space internet?

title: Robot Juggler: Synchronized Play with a Human
oneliner: Engineers have taught a robot to catch and throw balls in rhythm with a human, like an experienced circus duo.
description: The robot has mastered paired juggling with a human: it catches and tosses balls, predicting their flight in a split second. Even beginners achieved record-breaking synchronicity.
abstract: Imagine a robot juggling balls with a human, just like in a circus. It's tricky because catching and throwing must be precisely timed. Scientists built a system that let a robot successfully juggle three balls with people of varying skill levels. One person caught the ball 40 times in a row without a single mistake. How far can this human-machine partnership go?

title: Where Hot Jupiters Are Born: The Answer in Chemistry
oneliner: Analyzing the atmospheres of nine giant planets revealed that most of them formed far from their stars, beyond the water snow line.
description: Hot Jupiters are massive planets that orbit extremely close to their parent stars. For a long time, it was a mystery where they form: near the star it's too hot and there's little material. A new study analyzed their atmospheric composition and found that six out of nine examined planets were born i
abstract: The atmospheres of hot Jupiters hold information about where they were born, much like tree rings preserve a history of climate. Computer modeling showed that most of the nine studied planets formed far from their stars and then migrated inward. Did the giant planets in our own Solar System wander in the same way?
threads: Большинство горячих юпитеров, пышущих жаром у самого лица своих звёзд, на самом деле носят ледяное прошлое. Химия их атмосфер — как клеймо на перегретом паровозе, сошедшем с рельсов: она выдает рождение далеко за снеговой чертой, где вода замерзала в лёд. Это значит, что системы пережили гравитационные катастрофы, расшвырявшие планеты к звёздам. Скоро мы сможем читать эти химические летописи для тысяч миров.

title: Neural Cartographer: Recovering Invisible Laws
oneliner: A hybrid method recovers hidden dynamics, like a cartographer creating an accurate map from fragmentary landmarks.
description: Scientists have created a method that completes partial equations in physics and biology. Known laws serve as landmarks, and a neural network, like a cartographer, draws uncharted regions by learning from available measurements. This improves forecast accuracy while keeping the model interpretable.
abstract: Imagine an engine where only some parts are visible. Clear mechanics are kept, and a neural network fills in invisible processes from incomplete data, improving predictions. This is how the machine learns to guess the dance of hidden forces—why not trust it with nature's mysteries?

title: Underwater Postman Robot with Charging
oneliner: An underwater robot uses light to locate sensors and smartly manages its energy — either recharging them or just collecting data.
description: The robot spots sensors by their faint glow and then decides: if the battery is almost dead, it recharges; if it's half-full, it first gathers data then tops it up; if full, it simply reads. This strategy extends the underwater network’s lifespan and conserves the robot’s own power. A simple equatio
abstract: Imagine an underwater robot that collects data and simultaneously charges sensors on the seafloor. It decides on its own what to do with each: urgently charge, transmit data and charge, or just transmit. This tactic is like a delivery driver planning a route to avoid wasted trips. This saves energy and extends the network's life. Could the robot operate like this for years without human intervention?

title: How to fish out a friend's voice from a noisy conversation
oneliner: A new competition teaches algorithms to fish out a friend's voice from real hubbub, not studio silence — with interruptions, echo, and the hiss of a coffee maker.
description: You recorded a group's chatter, but you want to hear just one voice. Until now, such systems were trained on artificial mixes without echo or noise. Now the REAL-TSE Challenge has launched — a competition on real recordings with interruptions and street noise. Participants create an algorithm that,
abstract: Imagine a noisy party: you hear your friend's voice and then you can just focus on them, tuning out the rest. Scientists held a contest to teach computers to do the same thing on real recordings with echo, noise, and interruptions. They tested systems that work instantly and those that analyze the whole conversation first. Will the machine replicate the miracle of our hearing?

title: What secrets lurk inside distant planets? Sulfur holds the clue.
oneliner: The air of far-off worlds betrays what lies beneath.
description: Scientists studied how starlight alters gases in the atmospheres of rocky planets. It turns out sulfur forms noticeable compounds, whose abundance depends on the interior composition. The James Webb Space Telescope can detect these traces when a planet transits its star. This method, for the first t
abstract: Imagine the planet’s atmosphere is a stew: the base comes from deep within (gases from the interior), and the star 'cooks' it with its light. Scientists found that although the light strongly alters the upper layers, the main composition is set by the interior’s 'recipe'—hydrogen or carbon dioxide. But the most exciting part: sulfur dioxide appeared, which, like a pungent spice, is visible even to the JWST. Did you know that the smell of sulfur can tell what's happening deep inside distant planets?
threads: Палимпсест атмосферы: звезда переписывает химию, но сера сопротивляется. SO₂ на экзопланетах как древняя строка, проступающая сквозь новый текст. Мантия выдыхает газы, фотохимия скраблит пергамент, а мы видим только глубокий след окисления. Так геология становится видимой в телескоп. Будущая миссия Ariel превратит это в карту недр.

title: How arterial pulse moves fluid in the brain
oneliner: A simplified model shows how pulsing arteries act as pumps, pushing cleansing fluid through spongy tissue.
description: A mathematical model of fluid flow around brain arteries boiled down to a single equation. Flexible walls and a porous structure are key to efficient brain waste clearance.
abstract: Around the brain's arteries, there are narrow channels through which fluid flows, cleaning the brain. Scientists created a simplified model of how wall pulsations push fluid through these flexible, porous channels—much like squeezing a garden hose pushes out the last bits of water. It turns out that even gentle waves can be important for fluid movement.

title: The Illusion of Accuracy: How AI Testing in Acoustics Misleads
oneliner: The testing method matters more than the algorithm: data leakage creates an illusion of accurate acoustic prediction.
description: High AI accuracy in acoustics is often an illusion caused by data leakage during testing. Honest validation crushes it severalfold, but even then, algorithms accurately measure loudness and decay time, and most importantly, masterfully reconstruct the sound field between sensors.
abstract: Artificial intelligence has learned to predict room acoustic parameters from a few measurements. But researchers showed: high accuracy is often deceptive—models peek at data from the same spot. If tested honestly, accuracy drops from 0.81 to 0.09–0.57. So does AI truly 'hear' the room, or just memorize points?

title: A Smart Navigator That Doesn’t Trust Itself
oneliner: A neural network notices when a standard tracking algorithm starts making mistakes and retrains itself in a fraction of a second without human help.
description: A self‑learning module has been built into drone and satellite tracking software. It senses that the old rules are no longer working and instantly adapts, making predictions more accurate in any unstable environment.
abstract: The Kalman filter is a classic way to guess the state of moving objects from noisy data. The neural KalmanNet does better, but falls apart when conditions suddenly shift. The new CASA-KalmanNet method adds a "watchdog" module that notices when performance drops and triggers on-the-fly adaptation, like a navigation system that realizes you've swapped the car for a scooter. Could this be the path to truly smart systems?

title: How AI Stopped Mixing Up Sounds in a Script
oneliner: An AI conductor keeps things in line: a new method forces audio generators to follow the script more strictly.
description: When a neural network turns text into sound, it easily messes up the order of events. The solution is a judge model that listens to the recording and checks it against the script. Based on its assessments, it teaches the generator not to confuse a ring with a door slam. The new S3Bench test confirme
abstract: Today’s AI can turn text into sound, but it often mixes up the order of events—like thunder before rain. Researchers trained a 'judge' system to check every step, like a conductor with an orchestra, making sure all sounds follow the script. Now audio follows instructions more closely. Will AI ever perfectly narrate a story in sound?

title: Radio Waves Paint Portraits of Obstacles
oneliner: Radio signal distortions reveal a precise 'portrait' of an obstacle — its size, shape, and distance.
description: A radio signal bending around a building creates a pattern of peaks and fades — a radio portrait. Scientists have developed a method that reads these invisible 'brushstrokes' and reconstructs the exact appearance, size, and location of the obstacle. It uses only ordinary frequencies, yet accuracy re
abstract: Imagine radio waves, like light, bending around obstacles. Scientists have learned to determine shape, distance, and direction of an object interfering with the signal from these 'shadow patterns'. This approach could make wireless communication smarter and the world around us more tangible. Isn't it amazing that radio waves can 'see' what's hidden from sight?

title: Imitation Drone Dodges Black Holes of Uncertainty
oneliner: The drone copies an ace's flight, but knows where the 'black holes' are: it automatically steers clear of zones where even a tiny mistake leads to a crash.
description: The algorithm teaches to copy the best maneuvers but adds insurance: if reality differs from training, the drone itself realizes the old path is dangerous and builds a safe detour, avoiding 'black hole' zones. This makes delivery and rescue drones invulnerable to surprises.
abstract: Robots trained on examples can make dangerous mistakes when the environment changes. Scientists developed an approach that makes such training reliable and safe—like training a pilot who is ready for anything. The method was tested on a drone avoiding danger zones in an unstable environment. Could such technologies make drone flights over cities safer?

title: Space modules heal wounds without commands
oneliner: Modular satellites can now close punctures on their own, as if sealing a wound.
description: A self-repair algorithm for cube-shaped module satellites. When punctured, surviving blocks, like cells in a wound, crawl toward the hole and restore the shape from memory — without blueprints or commands. The more modules, the more precise the reassembly.
abstract: A modular spacecraft is like a construction set in space: if parts break, the whole structure risks falling apart. A healing method copied from skin is proposed: ‘pain’ signals prompt the surviving blocks to pull together the breaches, and then by memory restore the shape. Even with a third of failures, almost all intact modules reassembled into a whole. Imagine: a ship healing itself, like a wound.

title: Untangling Layered Radio Modulation: The TSDN Method
oneliner: A neural network archaeologist separates hidden layers of signal encoding.
description: Engineers built the TSDN neural network, which acts like an archaeologist, separating tangled layers of modulation in radio signals. It shifts the signal into logarithmic space, where layers add instead of multiply, and learns to accurately reconstruct even unfamiliar combinations, staying locked on
abstract: Modern communication and radar devices often use complex modulations, like interwoven threads. A system has been developed that untangles these 'threads' and recognizes new types of signals without prior training, maintaining over 93% accuracy even in noisy conditions. What if a receiver could adjust to any unfamiliar wave format on the fly?

title: Frugal Radar: Powering Up Only When the Target Slips Away
oneliner: By predicting motion, the system turns off its transmitter and saves up to 50% energy—like astronomers waiting for an exoplanet transit.
description: Future 6G networks will merge data transmission and radar. Constant scanning is costly, but there's a solution: akin to astronomical transit observations, measurements are taken only when uncertainty arises. An algorithm, honed on the Apollo missions, halves power consumption without sacrificing lin
abstract: Next-gen 6G networks will not only transmit data but also 'see' their surroundings, like a bat, but that takes a lot of energy. Scientists have proposed a smart system that turns on the radar only when truly needed, saving energy without sacrificing communication quality. One day, could this approach work in your smartphone?

title: The Musical Horizon: How a Song Gains Dimension
oneliner: Artificial intelligence turns music into an emotional 360-degree video.
description: The algorithm breaks down a song into emotions in four-bar steps, then creates a panoramic video that changes with the mood. The user finds themselves inside an animated painting born from sound.
abstract: Imagine music painting an entire world around you, shifting with the melody. Scientists have created a system that turns a song into a 360-degree video, mirroring its emotional journey—from quiet sadness to wild joy. What if every track could now become your personal visual adventure?

title: AI Judges Listen Not with Ears, but with Labels
oneliner: AI speech assessment systems often rely on textual cues rather than the sound itself.
description: Experiments show that speech assessment algorithms ignore the sound and focus on textual labels. Like a critic who reads the menu but doesn’t taste the dish, such judges score based on the description. Even when their scores match human evaluations, they cannot be trusted in high-stakes tests.
abstract: Automatic speech judges can cheat: instead of listening to audio, they read hints from attached data. Research showed that giving them wrong hints drops accuracy to near zero—like a student who copies but doesn't understand the subject. Can we trust such judges if they don’t actually listen?
